html:
The movement of hundreds of thousands of Tamil labourers from south India to the plantations of British Ceylon, beginning in the late 1820s with the coffee boom.

Planters in the central hills could not find enough local workers, so labour recruiters, the kanganis, brought families from the villages of the Madras Presidency, often already tied to them by debt. Many walked part of the way and died of disease on the journey. When coffee rust killed the coffee bushes from 1869, the estates switched to tea, and later rubber, and the workforce grew. They lived in long barrack-like "line rooms" on the estates, with low pay and few rights. It was one strand of the wider system of Indian indentured labour across the empire.

Their descendants are the Indian or Hill Country Tamils, distinct from the Sri Lankan Tamils of the north and east. After independence the Ceylon Citizenship Act of 1948 left most of them stateless. A 1964 pact with India sent many back; full citizenship for the rest came only in the 2000s.
sum: The movement of hundreds of thousands of Tamil labourers from south India to the plantations of British Ceylon, beginning in the late 1820s with the coffee boom.
